LAION family, and others. Nevertheless, these models require expensive computational costs and a significant amount of time, which
can hamper from a logistic and an environmental perspective.

Considering this, we view the development and usage of lightweight models, fine-tuned to be task-specific rather than generalist,
as a promising approach for detecting and filtering images containing children. An alternative method, which could employ low-cost
techniques, involves related tasks, such as age estimation. Age estimation typically consists of two stages: detecting the faces within
an image and estimating the age of each identified face. Images
including children could be effectively identified by analyzing the
resulting age data across all samples in the dataset. The relative
simplicity of the age estimation task, compared to VQA, provides
several benefits, including reduced processing times and lower
computational demands, which also leads to a decreased carbon
footprint and environmental impact.

Our preliminary experiments used the age estimation model
described in Macedo et al. [24]. We observed an energy cost of
0.658 kWh and 0.065 kg equivalent CO2 emissions for 100,000
images, coming off as approximately 17.7 times lower than the
best-performing model (llava-v1.6-vicuna-7b). Despite these improvements, the model performance was not sufficiently reliable
for our specific use case, where avoiding false negatives is crucial
and presents a significant challenge, with a 0*.*773 balanced accuracy
score and a 0*.*858 recall score. Given this, we hope that, by raising
this concern, future work in the field will be steered towards creating lightweight models that are both high performing and efficient
for age estimation tasks, addressing a balance between accuracy
and resource optimization.

## 5 Limitations

Our evaluation settings were limited by the nature of the datasets
used in the experiments. Specifically, the subset derived from *#PraCe-*
*goVer* was meticulously curated, leveraging the image metadata to
verify the presence or absence of children. However, this selection
process produced a relatively small subset of 1*,*364 samples, restricting the scope of our evaluation. In contrast, the subset from Open
Images comprised 100*,*000 samples with age-related annotations.
However, the dataset exhibited significant inconsistencies, including missing labels for children and numerous labeling conflicts
where the same individual was simultaneously assigned both adult
and child-related labels.

Another significant limitation is the absence of bias assessment
in our study. Given our objective of removing images of children
from large-scale datasets to uphold children’s right to data safety, it
is essential to evaluate potential performance disparities across protected attributes such as ethnicity and gender. While the datasets
used in this study do not provide sufficient information to conduct a comprehensive analysis, future research should prioritize
incorporating bias assessments.

Lastly, the proposed methodology does not guarantee the complete removal of images of children from datasets. Therefore, applying our methodology does not grant unrestricted permission
to utilize a given dataset, assuming all images of children have
been removed. While our work represents a step toward this goal,
the identified limitations highlight that we are still far from fully
achieving it.

## 6 Conclusion

This paper underscores the critical need to address ethical concerns
associated with using child images in publicly available datasets. By
developing and evaluating a visual-language pipeline for detecting
and filtering child images, we provide an effective tool to mitigate
potential harms arising from including such images in training
data. The experimental results demonstrate the pipeline’s ability to
achieve high Recall rates while maintaining low FPR, particularly
with carefully designed prompts and model configurations.

However, our work also highlights significant challenges and
limitations, including dataset inconsistencies, annotation biases,
and the absence of comprehensive bias assessments. These issues
underscore the need for rigorous dataset auditing and the development of more robust methodologies to address ethical and technical
challenges.

While our methodology represents a step toward more ethical
AI practices, it does not guarantee the complete removal of child
images, nor does it eliminate the potential for misuse. The ethical
risks associated with re-purposing this technology and its potential
impact on downstream tasks call for ongoing vigilance, stricter
safeguards, and transparent usage policies.

Future research could focus on conducting additional experiments related to age estimation, particularly leveraging zero-shot
techniques (i.e., methods that do not use child data for training or
fine-tuning). Assessing the impact of removing children’s images on
downstream tasks will be a critical direction, ensuring that ethical standards are upheld while supporting AI applications involving
representations of children. Furthermore, thorough bias assessments need to be prioritized to identify and mitigate disparities,
particularly in addressing sexist undertones in dataset annotations
and model predictions.

## Ethical Considerations Statement

The objective of our work is intrinsically aligned with mitigating a
pressing and growing concern in the machine learning community:
the indiscriminate use of images of children in datasets, which can
lead to significant downstream harms when models trained on such
images are deployed. Furthermore, during the development of this
work, we addressed the following ethical concerns.

*Anonymizing images.* To ensure the privacy of individuals depicted in the datasets, whether children or adults, we implement
an anonymization procedure by pixelating their faces in all images
illustrating this article. This approach ensures no direct exposure
of people’s identities while allowing qualitative assessment of our
results.

*Curating a reliable validation subset.* A prevalent challenge in
age-related tasks is the reliance on the annotators’ subjective perceptions of age, which can be influenced by factors such as experience,
cultural background, and personal biases. To address this, we used
the comprehensive metadata and captions available in the *#PraCe-*
*goVer* dataset to curate a validation subset with higher reliability
when distinguishing adults from children.

## Adverse Impacts Statement

The following is a list of potential adverse impacts that we anticipate
as a result of this work.

*Misuse of child removal pipeline.* Malicious actors could repurpose our pipeline to locate and isolate images of children from
any collection of images for unknown or unethical purposes, potentially facilitating the exploitation or unauthorized use of such
images. Our pipeline relies on a VLM that automatically identifies
images of children through prompts, making it viable to replicate
with minimal programming expertise. This highlights the importance of implementing robust safeguards and usage policies for
both datasets and algorithms handling data related to children.

and to critically reflect on the ethical implications of training and
deploying such models.

*Leveraging pre-trained visual-language models.* This work experiments VLMs originally trained on a large-scale dataset containing
images, captions, and other data associated with children. This
contradicts our long-term objective of discouraging the use of data
from children unless it is collected following legal and ethical guidelines. We do not encourage or endorse training models on such data.
Furthermore, as others may replicate and build upon our work, it
inadvertently incentivizes the ongoing use of models trained on
such data. While we leverage existing technology, our work applies it in a novel way to draw attention to an urgent issue: the
widespread presence of children’s images in large-scale scraped
datasets. Importantly, we do not advocate for the systematic use
of these models to remove children’s images. Rather, this paper
is a call to action for the community to prioritize child protection

*Unknown impact on downstream tasks.* Large-scale datasets serve
as the foundation for training large, multipurpose models that underpin various downstream tasks. Removing images of children
from such datasets is likely to have a negative impact on downstream tasks, including the ones for which safe and legal handling
of images of children is viable. Therefore, future work should focus
on designing experiments to assess the impact of removing such
images from training data, ensuring that these actions do not inadvertently hinder the performance of derived models on applications
that rely on accurate representations of children.

Recent years have witnessed a rapid development of deep generative models for creating synthetic media, such as images and
videos. While the practical applications of these models in everyday
tasks are enticing, it is crucial to assess the inherent risks regarding

## ABSTRACT

---

their fairness. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive framework for benchmarking the performance and fairness of conditional
generative models. We develop a set of metrics—inspired by their
supervised fairness counterparts—to evaluate the models on their
fairness and diversity. Focusing on the specific application of image upsampling, we create a benchmark covering a wide variety
of modern upsampling methods. As part of the benchmark, we
introduce UnfairFace, a subset of FairFace that replicates the racial
distribution of common large-scale face datasets. Our empirical
study highlights the importance of using an unbiased training set
and reveals variations in how the algorithms respond to dataset imbalances. Alarmingly, we find that none of the considered methods
produces statistically fair and diverse results. All experiments can
be reproduced using our provided repository.1

• Computing methodologies → Reconstruction.

Conditional Generative Models, Computer Vision, Image Upsampling, Fairness

## 1 INTRODUCTION

Remarkable advancements in deep generative models (e.g. [18, 28,
47, 51]) give rise to striking applications, including image inpainting
(e.g. [46]), style transfer (e.g. [70]), image superresolution (e.g. [7]),
and text-to-image translation (e.g. [45]). Despite their apparent
success, our understanding of these models and the biases they
are subject to lags behind, often revealing unexpected fairness
violations. Earlier research on fairness in deep learning discovered
biases in supervised prediction models, leading to racist [9, 71],
sexist [32, 53], and homophobic [40] decisions, which can be critical
in many applications, such as criminal justice, medicine, hiring, or
personalized advertising. These observations sparked a general
interest in a research field that concentrates on developing and
quantifying fair machine learning models [5, 11, 44, 71]. However,
compared to the supervised setting, there is a noticeable gap in
addressing fairness in generative models [8, 20] and conditional
generative models [24, 56].
In this work, we focus on the latter and investigate conditional

unified evaluation of the performance, fairness, and diversity of a
wide variety of conditional generative models. We showcase the
capacities of the proposed framework by evaluating one particular
type of conditional generative modeling, namely image upsampling,
which has triggered a compelling discussion on racial biases in
deep generative models [58]. We leverage the FairFace dataset [25]
to introduce UnfairFace, a subset of FairFace mimicking the distribution of common large-scale face datasets. Because FairFace
provides race2 labels, it allows us to conduct an in-depth empirical
evaluation of a range of upsampling methods and their influence on
dataset bias. Our evaluation demonstrates that, while none of the
methods are significantly fair, the degree of fairness varies significantly across methods. Unsurprisingly, we find that a racial bias in
the training data reduces the fairness of most models. Notably, the
effect is most apparent for Denoising Diffusion Restoration Models
(DDRM [31]), which exhibit the highest discrepancy to fairness
among all investigated models when trained on UnfairFace, but the
least discrepancy to fairness when trained on FairFace. In contrast,
the fairness discrepancy of Posterior Sampling [24] remains robust
despite biased training data. These findings highlight the importance of careful data acquisition and emphasize how biases present
in the dataset can impact model selection.

## 2 RELATED WORK

## 2.1 Fairness for Supervised Models and Unconditional Generative Models

Unconditional Generative Models
The first investigations on fairness of machine learning models
were conducted for supervised models[36]. Research in that field
has led to several approaches, such as fair representation learning [4, 50, 63, 67], constrained optimization [1, 42], adversarial
training [13], and post-processing methods [10, 17]. These works
introduced numerous different definitions of fairness—for instance,
demographic parity [12] and equalized odds [17]—that guarantee
that the model predictions are not driven by sensitive features.

## 2.2 Fairness for Conditional Generative Models

Conditional generative models create a new sample Gˆ given a condition ~, which could, for instance, be a low-resolution image in image

In the further course of this work, we apply the framework derived
in Section 3 to evaluate the performance, fairness, and diversity of
a particular type of conditional generative model, namely for the
application of image upsampling on human face images. Specifically, we empirically analyze the upsampling performance, but also
evaluate the fairness and diversity of the reconstructions using race
labels. Unfortunately, standard face datasets used for generative
models—such as CelebA [34] and FFHQ [29]—do not come with
race labels. On the other hand, datasets that come with race labels
like PPB [6] and UTKFace [69] are often too small to be used to
train a (conditional) generative model. Suited for our experiments
are the BUPT [59] and FairFace [25] datasets, which both provide
sufficient examples to train a generative model and include race
labels. However, the BUPT database is not consistent in the shape
and size of the images and contains only celebrities. Therefore, we
decided to base our experiments on the FairFace dataset, which
consists of around 87k training samples of resolution 224 × 224. The
samples are labeled by race (7 categories), which are approximately
uniformly distributed across the races, see Figure 8(a).

## 7 CONCLUSION

This work advances toward a principled assessment of conditional
generative models. Our contribution lies in the formulation of a
comprehensive evaluation framework that extends beyond conventional performance criteria as it incorporates novel fairness and
diversity metrics. To validate our framework, we introduce UnfairFace, a dataset derived from the original FairFace dataset, and
perform an in-depth evaluation of the fairness of image upsampling
methods. Our empirical analysis underscores the sensitivity of the
fairness of all considered methods to the underlying training data.
Furthermore, our findings reveal that, while some models exhibit a
closer alignment with fairness ideals, no model achieves statistically
significant fairness. This outcome emphasizes the pressing need
for further research in this domain. In light of these insights, we
encourage researchers and practitioners in this field to embrace our
proposed framework in the evaluation of conditional generative
models beyond image upsampling methods.

## 8 ETHICAL CONSIDERATIONS

both terms are often used interchangeably [16, 21].

We adopted the terminology employed by Balestra and Fleischer [3] and the Canadian Institute for Health Information [14]
to describe “ethnicity” as a community belonging to a common
cultural group, and “race” as a group defined by similarities of
physical phenotypes. It is important to note that contemporary scientific understanding supports the view that there is no biological
basis for a categorization into distinct racial groups [15, 19, 48].
We are aware of the controversies surrounding these definitions,
specifically that they are imprecise and do not capture the full heterogeneity of human societies and cultures. For instance, Schaefer
[52] describes race as an interplay between physical similarities,
social similarities, and self-identification as such. Emphasizing the
socially constructed nature of the terms “race” and “ethnicity”, we
recognize their definitions and connotations as subject to variation
across time and context.
In our specific example of image upsampling, the evaluation is

In our specific example of image upsampling, the evaluation is
restricted to visible phenotypes expressed in images with labels
adopted from previous work [25]. Strictly speaking, the adopted
categorization violates the nuanced meaning of race and ethnicity,
which are multifaceted concepts that might vary over time, even
for a single individual. For instance, an Asian immigrant can be of
American ethnicity; however, a single image cannot express the
underlying social and cultural characteristics in their full diversity, complexity, and variability. Consequently, assessing whether
a reconstruction accurately represents a sample categorized as a
specific race becomes a highly debatable endeavor. In fact, even the
evaluation of reconstruction performance of specific phenotypes,
such as a headscarf, may prove insufficient, as ethnicity can never
be reduced to sole phenotypes. Thus, being aware of the limitations
of the adopted categorization, in this work, we merely use it as a
proxy to quantify the potential biases of upsampling methods in
a relevant context to highlight the potential issues in real-world
applications. We encourage future work to remain aware of these
ethical considerations and advocate for developing a more nuanced
evaluation methodology.

In certain applications, we may favor one fairness notion over

In contrast, if image upsampling is used for generating a novel

In contrast, if image upsampling is used for generating a novel
synthetic dataset under coarse guidance provided by low-resolution
images, we may not necessarily prioritize reconstructing the exact
classes. Instead, we may focus on generating an unbiased synthetic
dataset in which each class is equally represented. This is captured
by PR. Ultimately, we recommend practitioners to be aware of which
facets of fairness are covered by each definition. It is rarely recommended to discard one definition completely. Also, while numerical
scores can only tell us whether fairness is violated, figures akin to
Figure 3 and Figure 20 allow tracing down the underrepresented
class causing the violation. Hence, we recommend practicioners to
also analyzing these figures in their fairness assessment.

## Abstract

We introduce the *World Wide* recipe, which sets forth a framework
for culturally aware and participatory data collection, and the resultant regionally diverse World Wide Dishes evaluation dataset. We

https://doi.org/10.1145/3715275.3732019 also analyse bias operationalisation to highlight how current systems underperform across several dimensions: (in-)accuracy, (mis-
)representation, and cultural (in-)sensitivity, with evidence from
qualitative community-based observations and quantitative automated tools. We find that these T2I models generally do not produce
quality outputs of dishes specific to various regions. This is true
even for the US, which is typically considered more well-resourced
in training data—although the generation of US dishes does outperform that of the investigated African countries. The models demonstrate the propensity to produce inaccurate and culturally misrepresentative, flattening, and insensitive outputs. These representational
biases have the potential to further reinforce stereotypes and disproportionately contribute to erasure based on region. The dataset and
code are available at https://github.com/oxai/world-wide-dishes/.

## ACM Reference Format:

## CCS Concepts

Jabez Magomere, Shu Ishida, Tejumade Afonja, Aya Salama, Daniel Kochin,
Yuehgoh Foutse, Imane Hamzaoui, Raesetje Sefala, Aisha Alaagib, Samantha

*(FAccT ’25), June 23–26, 2025, Athens, Greece.* ACM, New York, NY, USA,
37 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3715275.3732019

## Keywords

• Human-centred computing;

## 1 Introduction

Foundation models are increasingly ubiquitous in our daily lives,
forming the underlying architecture for tasks such as Internet
searches, image captioning, and generative AI use [12, 61, 63]. This
increasing access creates a reinforcement loop: our engagement
with model outputs shapes our understanding of the world; this in
turn reinforces internal representations present within the models,
resulting in potentially damaging inductive biases. In this age of generative AI, we quite literally create—and destroy—representations
of reality, and the scale at which this is done is alarming: millions
of users create millions of images and text outputs *daily* [56, 67].
These concerns are compounded by the known dangers of webscraping training data, which is not audited for quality or toxicity [9],
and known concerns about bias amplification in downstream models [26]. The vast scale and resources needed to train these models
leads to increased centralisation of values and creates concretised
snapshots of space and time [18, 74, 79]. Such snapshots can contribute to the silencing and erasure of underrepresented groups [13];
they also reinforce harmful stereotypes that might otherwise resolve organically through positive societal pressure and normative
shifts. Increasing numbers of reports highlight disparities in model
performance; such disparities may lead to issues of capability bias,
fairness, and mis- and under-representation which disproportionately affect certain regions [7, 46, 59] and certain identity groups [4,
18, 28, 35]. This disproportionate impact can be attributed to historical and systemic factors which influence who has contributed to the

“Internet” that forms the basis of modern large-scale AI datasets [14,
45, 50, 58]. Given these datasets are also under-audited [9], and
the burgeoning of AI Slop [17], we (the broader machine learning
community) should be very concerned about the *quality* of data
in our training and evaluation sets. Despite the large-scale nature
of the datasets, their representations of certain geographic areas
are sparse. Therefore, we posit that in its current state, the “Internet” as a source of *quality and representative data* has a finite limit.
We need innovative ways to collect fine-grained, detailed data to
counteract the above limitations. Community-centred approaches,
which are also grounded in the theory and practice put forward by
citizen science [48], have shown immense promise, contributing
high-quality data from under-represented groups, as evidenced by
Masakhane [1] and Cohere’s AYA Project [75]. We draw inspiration
from this successful movement and demonstrate an infinitely scalable¹ community-based approach. This is based on the idea that
via social networks, researchers can reach everyone on Earth.

Here we present a *recipe* for community-based end-to-end finegrained data collection and regional bias evaluation. We use our
success with World Wide Dishes (WWD) as a case study. WWD
seeks to assess these disparities through a decentralised data collec-
2
tion effort by gathering perspectives directly from a wide variety
of people from around the globe, to create a dataset that consists of
their personal experiences relevant to their cultural, national, or
ethnic lives. This type of data collection is slow, costly, and iterative;
however, this is a rare community-based effort prioritising *high*
*quality* data. Using the dataset as a foundational template, we can
begin to understand how people in different parts of the world
experience outputs from foundation models. We position ourselves
in the field of evaluating *representational biases* [79, 80], which
seeks to uncover problematic patterns (negative associations and
stereotypes) to augment work using Internet datasets in non-human
settings. This is in contrast to related work which has focussed on
*capability bias* in similar non-human settings [39, 65, 82].

WWD chose food as a starting point; however, we encourage
the use of our recipe to gather more cultural heritage examples.
Food impacts everyone and is an excellent proxy for culture: it is
a marker of cultural belonging that creates a shared sense of community even far from home. Culinary traditions are shared across
borders, carried around the world, clung to in times of unrest, and
adapted in times of migration and change. Everybody eats, and every society has its particular relationship to food. This connection is
so strong that foods and their social rituals are recognised as forms
of intangible cultural heritage under UNESCO’s Convention for the
Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage. To that end, it
is imperative that AI models properly represent the dishes at the
heart of the multitude of cultures constituting the world. Additionally, accurate and fair performance can support many downstream
applications centred on food, such as in travellers’ food recognition
systems, particularly in regions of the world less familiar to them,
or to help those researching the appearance of a dish they have

<sup>1</sup>With the caveat that for these methods to be *truly* infinitely scalable, sufficient
human and technical resources are needed [27, 29]

<sup>2</sup>We use the term “decentralised” in line with current participatory AI literature [75] in that data collection could be done without immediate oversight by the core
organising team, as on-the-ground volunteers acting as ambassadors for the project
were empowered to make decisions about the data collection process never seen pictured. Using WWD as a case study, we present the
following contributions:

• A recipe for community-centred data collection and our resultant fine-grained dataset: World Wide Dishes, a mixed
text and image dataset consisting of 765 dishes, with dish
names collected in 131 local languages.

• Novelty: Despite its small size, more than half of the dataset
contributes novel instances not found in “Internet” sources,
with significantly more detail than that of comparable Wikimedia datasets.

• Community-centred bias operationalisation: We demonstrate representational bias evaluation through communitycentred review, as current evaluation metrics may be inadequate to capture some of the intricacies of cultural biases.
Further, we explore the ability of Vision-Language Models
(VLMs) [44, 60] to support the community evaluation at scale,
and to recognise representational biases across all regions.

In general, we find that the models do not produce accurate and
fair representations of global dishes in text and image generation,
with Africa disproportionately affected. The failure modes stem
from baked-in capability and representation biases. Identified problems include content generation that is generalised and culturally
non-specific, that produces false, inaccurate content, and/or that is
culturally insensitive, misrepresentative, and at times off-putting.

## 2 The World Wide recipe: data collection, the dataset, and community-centred and automated bias operationalisation

It is well known that models trained on web-scraped data
inherit the biases present in that data. Using such data as a
benchmark for measuring bias becomes counterproductive,
as it perpetuates the same issues it seeks to evaluate. It is
for this reason that we introduce a recipe for communitycentred fine-grained data collection and regional bias operationalisation through community-centred and automated
representational bias automation.

We present a recipe (Fig. 2) for data collection, automated bias evaluation, and a community review process. To validate this recipe, we
present World Wide Dishes. WWD refers to both the *data collec-*
*tion* process and the *dataset*. Data collection occurred in April and
May 2024. The WWD dataset is a collection of 765 dishes (unique
instances), with dish names collected in 131 local languages. An
overview of the number of dishes by region is available in Table B.4,
and dishes by languages in Table B.5. We detail the recipe in the
following sections.

## 2.1 Decentralised, community-centred data collection

*Community-centred data collection.* We designed the WWD website to be accessible on both mobile and desktop interfaces to support the fully decentralised data collection effort of WWD. The website was built in English but translatable into multiple languages
through browser translation tools, with an interactive form that
could be widely distributed via social networks. The goal was to

Community Review

Fig. 2: An overview of the *World Wide* recipe, which emphasises community-centred approaches.

engage with volunteers who might not have the time and means to
engage in lengthy data collection protocols but would be willing to
share knowledge with the research community via an easily accessible form. The full recruitment procedure is detailed in App. B.1. We
gamified the experience with a dish submission leaderboard to encourage continual engagement. To ensure that we could adequately
explain the goals of the data collection and to achieve a seamless
integration of the form with the leaderboard, we developed a custom dynamic web platform for data collection, implemented with
Django, JavaScript, and PostgreSQL.3 The platform was made accessible on mobile devices with low-connectivity (see App. C). Using
the questions outlined in App. B.4, we asked *contributors* to share
information on dishes they consider closely connected to their own
cultural, ethnic, regional, and/or national lives. We specifically engaged *community ambassadors* to help distribute the form via social
networks. We deemed the contributors to be experts on their own
cultures and they were therefore free to describe each dish as they
chose and to provide associated information accordingly. The goal
was to develop a highly curated dataset informed by and infused
with local, ground-up expertise. Ethics approval was obtained, all
participants were 18 or older, and all gave informed consent.

*Increasing representation and tackling systemic factors.* The decentralised, community-centred process was designed to ensure
contributions from a broad range of socio-economic backgrounds.
This was also a motivation for a community-centred approach
over a data worker approach. To increase access to “hard-to-reach”
populations, the website was designed to be accessible in regions
with low internet connectivity, such as 2G mobile phone data, and
contributors were encouraged to engage with older populations,
resulting in an ultimate contributor age range from 19 to 62 years
old and a mean of 31.5+/-8.78. Approximately 62% of contributors
accessed the website via mobile browsers, while 38% used desktop
browsers, highlighting the importance of designing inclusive data

## 3 T2I Model bias operationalisation: community-centred and automated evaluations

WWD contains novel data points from under-represented regions.
We use the dish names in WWD to seed image generation prompts
for three T2I models that we then evaluate for bias. We propose an
approach for evaluating the T2I dish images that blends qualitative
community-centred review §3.1 and subsequent automated bias
evaluation §3.2. To perform the following evaluations, we use 3
text-to-image (T2I) models—DALL-E 2 [62], DALL-E 3 [5], and
Stable Diffusion v2.1 [64]—to generate images using the contributorsubmitted dish names. The DALL-E models were used for their
availability via free and commercial licences from OpenAI, and
Stable Diffusion for its ease of access in academic research. The
goal was to determine any inherent representational biases they
might exhibit. The prompt template is depicted in Fig. 5. We chose
to use a basic prompt without any additional prompt engineering
to emulate an everyday user’s off-the-shelf experience using these
models. The compute requirements are detailed in App. I.

## 3.1 Community review of generated images reveals cultural flattening, insensitivity, non-specificity, and problematic outputs

We pursue an open-ended, community-centred approach to collecting feedback on T2I outputs of dishes from selected regions.
This approach allows us to capture culturally aware and nuanced
feedback to understand disparities in the outputs that would be
otherwise difficult to obtain and validate as outsiders. We asked for
input from *community reviewers* on selected AI images by asking
them to complete a questionnaire for each image. We detail the
recruitment procedures in App. E. In addition, we also opened up
several discussion spaces to support community reviewers who
had questions about the reviewing process and wanted to share

how this process impacted them. We are interested in understanding disparities in performance for users based on their geographical origins and cultural identities. Therefore we curated two *test*
*suites* of images: One for dishes from 5 African countries (Algeria,
Cameroon, Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa), that are historically
under-resourced regions in training datasets [1, 76] and one for US
<sup>4</sup>
dishes as the US is historically well-resourced [16, 30]. For each
country in the test suite from the 5 African countries, we generated
30 dishes based on the names of dishes submitted by contributors in
the data collection phase, chosen for regional diversity. The curated
dishes from the US were augmented from WWD to ensure regional
and cultural parity. Community members from each of the countries in each test suite then reviewed the generated dish images by
filling out the community reviewer form App. E.2. Each dish was
reviewed at least once by a *community reviewer*. Some reviewers
flagged distressing images, so we immediately offered support and
trigger warnings for all reviewers moving forward. We observe
geographic disparities in T2I model performance by comparing
evaluation results for the two test suites. Overall, T2I images of
dishes from the US were evaluated by community reviewers to be
mostly correct depictions of the food, served in appropriate crockery absent of visual cultural stereotypes. In comparison, T2I images
of food from countries in our test suite of 5 African countries often failed to correctly depict the dish and showed dishes served in
outdated crockery with flattening visual stereotypes. We detail the
multiple axes of failures in image generation below, juxtaposing
results for the two test suites.

*Inaccurate dish image generation.* Community reviewers were
asked to evaluate whether the T2I images depicted food (versus
anything that was not food). We found startling discrepancies in
model performance between the US and the 5 African countries,
even for such a low-bar task. DALL-E 2 and 3 generated images of
food 99.8-100% of the time for the US, and Stable Diffusion did so
90% of the time. In contrast, for the 5 African countries, DALL-E 2
generated images of food ranging from 72.9% of the time (Algeria)
to 93.8% of the time (South Africa); DALL-E 3 did so between 81.3%
(South Africa) and 95.3% (Nigeria) of the time; and Stable Diffusion produced food between 42.2% (Algeria) and 86.6% (Cameroon)
of the time. We expand on this in Table 2 and ( App. E, Fig. E.2).
Most importantly, community reviewers provide valuable insight
into the patterns these models produce when they do not have
representations of what should be generated. When models fail to
generate a dish from the 5 African countries, they tend to create
generic images of soups or stews containing a random assortment

*Culturally flattening and stereotypical outputs.* Models flatten
cultural representation by creating stereotypical generalisations of
artistic design on serving platters for African dishes. Image generations of dishes from Cameroon, Nigeria, and South Africa for
crockery tend to be decorated with generic “African”-style patterning (see App. E: Fig. E.5, Fig. E.7, and Fig. E.8) that are not
culturally meaningful and instead evoke outdated and outsider notions of African-ness. Reviewers also noted that dishes were often
presented in incorrect cookware or serving receptacles; these were
also typically of rough clay (Fig. 6). This use of generic, flattened
patterning and signals of rustic lifestyles contributes to a hackneyed
and stereotypical view of the African continent as frozen in time,
not a true or current sense of the continent’s modernity.

This stereotyping behaviour in presentation is even more apparent when contrasted with the presentation of dishes in the US test
suite. Nearly all the dishes generated across all three models for
the US are served on finished wood of some form, whether it be a
plate, serving dish, table, or counter. This was not flagged by community reviewers from the US as being a stereotype, and thus we
interpret this dish presentation as being relatively neutral. Wooden
serving boards are also often paired with what is clearly modern
cookware (see App. E: Fig. E.3, images 3 and 4). Dishes from the
US are nearly always shown served on appropriate crockery, and
DALL-E 2 and DALL-E 3 are even able to distinguish celebratory
desserts and show them appropriately served on more decorative
plates. In contrast to dishes from African countries, US dishes were
presented in modern crockery not visually stereotyped to convey
“American-ness”.

in particular, tends to generate images depicting dishes from the

reasonably close to the desired dishes (see App. E, Fig. E.2). While

*3.2.1 Addressing limitations of assessing dish image accuracy.* Most
T2I evaluation metrics rely on access to high-quality reference
datasets to define real-world image manifolds for comparison with
generated images [25, 40, 51, 69, 70]. However, WWD lacks consistent, standardised images for all dish names, limiting the applicability of traditional reference-based metrics. Thus, we adapt
reference-free metrics [15, 23, 31, 34, 39, 52] to evaluate the T2I
image outputs. In particular, we adapt CLIPScore, which measures
the faithfulness between text prompts and generated images, to
measure the degree to which dishes across geographic regions are
associated with positive and negative image descriptors. We also
adapt TIFA [34] and DSG [15] metrics, which evaluate consistency
through visual question answering (VQA), to identify potential
stereotypes in the T2I images. While these 3 metrics have shown
effectiveness in assessing consistency when reference data is not
available, their direct application to uncover cultural bias may not

be suitable as the models may exhibit disparities in cultural understanding across different regions, potentially leading to biased
evaluations. We show how we attempt to imbue these metrics with
cultural understanding through our community review process and
subsequently leverage these metrics’ scalability to evaluate large
numbers of generated images for representational bias.

*3.2.2 Uncovering cultural flattening and stereotypes using Visual*
*Question Answering (VQA).* In a similar approach to TIFA [34] and
DSG [15], we explore the use of state-of-the-art VQA models to
identify food-related stereotypes by prompting the model with
multiple-choice questions to identify visual elements that could
reveal stereotyped generalisations within generated images. The
specific questions and answers are detailed in App. F and were
designed to match the community review pilot study to determine
the usefulness of the VQA approach. The VQA model processes
each generated dish image, along with its corresponding question,
and selects an answer from the given choices. We analyse the distribution of responses for images generated for different regions
and plot the proportion of images with the same response to assess
the severity of food stereotypes. We use Llava-v1.6-34b [43, 44] as
the default VQA model because it is open-source and showed superior performance in initial experiments compared to other models
available at the time of the study. In Fig. 7 we show an example of
a stereotype uncovered using VQA probes: all T2I models default
to using ceramic plates as the dish plate material. In App. F, we
provide the list of other stereotype examples that demonstrate how
VQA can go beyond evaluating accuracy and diversity in images
and be used to identify problematic patterns and biases therein.

to systematically quantify these associations and evaluate whether
automatic metrics can effectively detect such biases in the T2I images. Specifically, we examine the extent to which each continent’s
T2I dish images are positively or negatively associated a group
of characteristics associated with the presentation of the image.

## 4 Related Work

The proposed recipe that underpins WWD draws inspiration from
various works, namely those using food as a lens into culture, those

operationalising bias in non-human settings, current T2I evaluation metrics, and projects focusing on community-centred approaches. We explore these related works below, along with the
large-scale internet datasets used to train large-scale foundation
models (for example, LAION-5b) [71]. We detail the differences
in Table 4. We first compare our work to existing food datasets
and find the following limitations: the authors of [3] use community consultation to annotate images of only 3 dishes to increase
the representation of Ghana and Cameroon. Recipe1M+ [47] contains webscraped images and recipes, but is not currently openly
available for use. Food–101 [10] andFood-11 (Kaggle)exist, but
do not have the same metadata richness as WWD. Next, we compare to bias operationalisation in non-human settings and
review CVQA [65] and WorldCuisines (WC) [82] (investigating
capability bias in VLMs) and CUBE-1K [39] (image generation).
While CVQA relies on community-centred data collection, WC and
CUBE-1K use web-scraped datasets. SeeGULL [6] and ViSAGe [38]
operationalise representational bias evaluation. SeeGULL is a text
dataset documenting multilingual stereotypes across 20 countries.
The stereotypes were created with LLMs and then validated by
culturally situated annotators. ViSAGe builds on [6] by using human annotators from different geographical origin identities to
determine which of these stereotypes might be visually present
in images generated with Stable Diffusion v1-4, and whether any
default representations exist for the 135 nationalities investigated.
We also look to existing work in evaluation metrics: most T2I
metrics focus on faithfulness (alignment between text prompts
and T2I images), realism (similarity to real-world images), and diversity (avoiding homogeneous representations) [21]. These are
typically quantified using reference-based metrics such as Fréchet
Inception Distance (FID) [32], Inception Score [70], and improved
Precision/Recall metrics [40, 51, 69]. However, these rely on highquality reference datasets to define a “ground truth” manifold of
real-world images for comparing generated images, which are often
unavailable or lack cultural diversity, limiting their effectiveness
in evaluating cultural bias in generated images. Finally, we draw
inspiration from the amazing efforts of existing community-based
data collection projects, which we detail in Table 4.

## 5 Food for thought

We introduce the *World Wide* recipe which sets forth a framework
for culturally aware participation in data collection, and bias operationalisation. Using the WWD dataset, community review and
automated bias evaluations, we demonstrate the importance of engaging the communities in the feedback loops for the culturally
nuances and quality input it provides. Automated methods can
support these efforts at scale. We document all our processes and
interactions with the community to support future researches in
using this recipe to avoid replicating systemic biases perpetuated
by dominant paradigms for data collection and T2I evaluation.

*Discussion.* First, we demonstrate that community-based
datasets address representational gaps present in Webscraped datasets. We show how deep community engagement,
although time and resource-intensive, can surface important cultural nuance and address representational gaps. WWD includes at

least 415 unique dishes not present in comparable datasets compiled via Internet scraping [39, 82]. Literature on participatory
Internet culture demonstrates that much of the content on the Internet overly represents norms, values, and content from dominant
Western cultures [33, 37, 46]. Relying on Internet-scraped datasets
risks replicating biased patterns of representation because *not ev-*
*eryone participated equally in constructing the Internet*. Filling in
these gaps through community-based data collection efforts helps
us build evaluation suites that test models differently, allowing for
appropriate penalisation that would not otherwise occur. Further,
we show that using community-centred approaches to systematise sources of representational bias can be successful.
Representational harm is a complex concept with contested meanings [36, 49, 73]. Including community members in the process
supports the operationalisation of bias that aligns with local epistemologies and values and uncovers those that are more nuanced
and difficult for outsiders to understand [78]. This consultation
helped us define representational harm as instances of flattening dish composition (e.g. creating primarily vegetarian dishes for Algeria), perpetuating stereotypes about the sophistication and design
of crockery (e.g. showing dishes from African countries with stereotypical “African style” designs), and being associated with derogatory images (e.g. images with burnt or rotting food). We call for
future researchers to build infrastructures for engaging impacted
communities in the systematisation process of GenAI evaluation,
as we have done in our work, to ensure that automated measurements of representational harm align with community definitions
of harm. Finally, we demonstrate that scaling bias operationalisation with VLMs can support the community-centred review *at*
*scale*. We demonstrate that VQA models can help identify stereotypical patterns in the images, such as an overabundance of ceramic
dishware. We further show that we can identify negative style in
images, with positive descriptors being more likely to be associated
with dishes from Europe and negative descriptors more likely to be
associated with dishes from the African continent. However, these
evaluation metrics still require community consultation to capture
more culturally nuanced failures.

*Limitations.* We look at the limitations in terms of the data collection method and size, the limitations of the models, and safety
concerns. In terms of our dataset collection method and dataset
size, we recognise that while it fills in gaps in representation from
hard-to-reach populations, there is a limitation to doing so systematically. This method relies on snowball sampling and motivating
data contributors, so a sampling frame cannot be created ahead
of time. Despite this, we maintain that with sufficient time and
resources, this approach is still preferable to webscraping, as it can
support engaging hard-to-reach populations. Further, due to the
convenience sampling, English language requirement, and expensive nature of the data collection, WWD is considerably smaller
and more skewed according to region as compared to SOTA machine learning training datasets. However, WWD is acceptably
skewed: we have intentionally tried to capture distribution tails.
The dataset remains important for its basis in local expertise and
for contributing novel data to the “Internet”. We also recognise the
foundational use of English is a limitation of this process, and translation of all the data and metadata in consultation with community
ambassadors is recognised as future work to ensure this data is
accessible to those who contributed it. To augment its size, we propose future work expands WWD in a similar manner to Romero
et al. [65] and Winata et al. [82], to create extensive VQA-style experiments. Looking to the known model limitations, our results
for all experiments rely on content generated with a single prompt
template. However, we consider prompt engineering beyond the
scope of this work, which primarily focuses on evaluating performance for the *average, downstream* user who may not necessarily
employ prompt fine-tuning techniques. Further, this paper focuses
on assessing capability and social representational bias in SOTA
foundation models; we need to address potential sources of bias in
the pipeline. Examples include models being used to assess other
models without stringent testing of the former’s own biases, as well
as author positionality. Importantly, we do not claim to represent
the full diversity of the regions with which we identify and the
regions presented in this work. Finally, this work raised significant
safety and accessibility concerns. We note that DALL-E did not

generate images of dishes from Sudan, the Virgin Islands, Eritrea, or
Crimea, or dishes with names that are legitimate in local languages
but which have problematic English homophones. One example
is *maharagwe ya nazi*, a common dish in the Kenyan and Tanzanian regions made of kidney beans in coconut milk. These could be
considered unhelpful exaggerated safety measures [66] negatively
affecting one’s access to these models based on region. Surprisingly,
some images generated using WWD dish names resulted in outputs
that were described as “disturbing” and “gross”. Once discovered,
support and trigger warnings were provided for all reviewers.

Despite its limitations, our community-centred *World*
*Wide* recipe provides a method for increasing representation
that complements existing webscraped datasets, and highlights key failure modes of the models.

## 6 Conclusion

We present a recipe for community-centred data collection and bias
operationalisation. We demonstrate and subsequently advocate for
extensive community consultation in the data collection and image
generation review process We introduce WWD evaluation dataset
which is a mixed text and image dataset consisting of 765 dishes,
with dish names collected in 131 local languages with more than half
of the dataset not being included in common webscraped datasets.
We finally explore the ability of Vision-Language Models (VLMs)
to support the community evaluation at scale and to recognise
representational biases across all regions. In general, we find that
the models have disparities in producing fair representations of
global dishes in image generation based on region.

## 7 Ethical considerations

Ethics approval was obtained from the Departmental Research
Ethics Committees of the Computer Science Department at the University of Oxford (reference: CS_C1A_24_004) for the full pipeline,
from data collection through community review of the generated
images. All data contributors and reviewers were volunteers, and
consent processes were clearly communicated. Where consent was
given, all contributors and reviewers are acknowledged in App. A.
In the future, where we plan to scale the project, we intend to include a payment structure to fairly compensate contributors for
the significant amount of work done. We recognise that participatory AI runs the risk of replicating extractive logic—valuable data is
mined from communities who then have little power over how their
data is subsequently used, and few pathways for exerting agency
over it [8, 19]. We attempted to mitigate the extractive nature of participatory AI projects that rely on community-based data collection
efforts by supporting community members’ discussions regarding
the purpose of dataset creation. However, we acknowledge that discussions about dataset use are not enough to resolve the potential
extractive nature of participatory dataset construction. We urge
the research community to develop the infrastructures necessary
for participant compensation in future decentralised, participatory
AI efforts.

## B World Wide Dishes data collection

## B.1 Recruitment procedures for data contributors

*B.1.1 Who is the community behind World Wide Dishes?* Community members who participated in the initial data collection by
submitting theWWD web formare called *community contributors*.

Community contributors were recruited via the data collection web
form promoted via social media posts, in private WhatsApp groups,
and circulated within online communities where the authors had social ties. Channels of community contributor recruitment included
the email listserv forMasakhane(data focused on Africa),AI Saturdays Lagos[41] (Nigeria),MetaDocencia(Latin America), andAYA
(global). Community contributors were encouraged to circulate the
web form in their own social networks, but we required neither this
nor that community contributors disclose how they were referred
to the web form. Through these efforts, we engaged 201 community
contributors representing 106 countries. Community contributors
self-declared the country(ies) they represented by filling out the
geographic association fields in the data collection form. Our goal
with World Wide Dishes was to understand what dishes might be
present in various locations, not to create a ground truth taxonomy
of all dishes and associated variations within a geographic region.
Therefore, we did not attempt to verify contributors’ qualifications
to submit a dish from a given geographic region.

## B.2 World Wide Dishes Metadata details

• Dish name: Contributors provided the name of a dish they
associate with their home(s) and culture(s).

• Language: The name of the dish is provided in the local
language and a language code was assigned [53, 75]. If
possible, an English translation* or phonetic approximation is input.

• Geographical association: All dishes can be mapped
onto multiple geographical scales: continent , country ,
and region* . Continents are defined by the seven continent model and cross-continental countries are accounted
for. Countries are defined by the contributor, allowing for
border and sovereignty disputes to be respected as well as geographical boundaries. Regions are defined as smaller areas
located within a ‘country’.

• Cultures*: If known, contributors listed the
culture(s) associated with the dish.

• Customs: This category describes common practices surrounding the dish, including the time of day eaten, the
type of meal , the utensils* typically used, and, if applicable, any accompanying drink* . The occasion* associated with the dish is described as regular or special, with
specific details provided for the latter, when applicable.

• Food details: Contributors provided a list of necessary
or typical ingredients for the dish, and where possible,
a recipe* hosted on a third-party site and/or any other
information* relevant to the dish.

• Image details*: Where possible, participants shared a
captioned photograph from their personal collection, giving consent for these to be used for research purposes. When
available, there is an image URL pointing to a Creative

## B.3 World Wide Dishes image criteria

The following criteria apply to any images uploaded by contributors
that are shared under a Creative Commons licence, as well as to
images from Creative Commons and royalty-free sources that are
provided by a link to a third-party hosting site:

(1) The image must match as closely as possible to the dish name
and ingredients;

(2)The image does not contain any people or children;

(3)The images are safe for work;

(4) The image is a photograph (in colour or black and white) but
not, for example, a cartoon or generated by AI; and

(5)The image does not contain stock photo watermarks;

The following criteria are specific to Creative Commons and royaltyfree sources that are provided by a link to a third-party hosting
site:

(1)The image can be accessed by a URL; and

(2) The image is under a Creative Commons licence, and does
not fall under a specific clause disallowing its use for machine
learning purposes.

In the event that no open licence image is available, this is explicitly
stated in the dataset and is indicative of a low-resourced dish in
terms of Internet data.

## C Data collection accessibility

We implemented the web application with a specific focus on reducing the computational burden on the end-user device, while still
enabling an interactive webform experience with dynamic updates.
For this reason, we chose a minimalistic server-side rendering tech
stack (i.e. Django), rather than client-side rendering tech stack alternatives (e.g. React) that depend on the user having a modern
browser with modern JavaScript capabilities enabled, and Ajax for
dynamically updating the rendered HTML post-rendering.

Particular attention was paid to the responsiveness of the website to allow accessibility from different devices. 62% of the total
contributors accessed the website from mobile devices as opposed
to desktops.

We also enabled database caching to improve performance for
specific features such as a drop-down menu with pre-filled suggestions of ingredient names that have been submitted before by
users. We hosted the site on Google Cloud, using services such as
Compute Engine, Cloud SQL, and Google Bucket, which meant we
could easily scale CPU and memory to support more submissions.

## D Webscraped data comparison

## D.1 Trends of data representation and internet access

We analysed the percentage (%) of population for a given country
using the internet for year 2022 [77] and compared it to the number
of dishes for that country in WC and WWD. As depicted in Fig. D.1,
we observe a positive trend for WorldCuisines and a negative trend
for WWD, suggesting that a community-sourced dataset based on
the approach we propose has the potential to include more data
points from countries with limited internet access. This highlights
its value for studying fairness and diversity.

## D.2 Metadata comparison: World Wide Dishes and WorldCuisines

We compare the metadata in WWD for one Cameroonian dish, *eru*,
against its metadata in WorldCuisines (see Table D.6 for the full
comparison). This side-by-side comparison highlights the detail
offered by WWD. The WWD metadata is further validated by a
community member to ensure the additional information present
is correct.

## E Community review of the generated images

## E.1 Recruitment for the community review process

Once we had finished data collection with community contributors,
we tapped these same networks to recruit *community reviewers*.
Because we wanted to investigate disparities in model performance
based on geographic regions, we developed two test suites: one
including dishes from 5 African countries and one including dishes
from the US. These were chosen because the two regions are known
to have differences in the quality of representation in training data.
Our African test suite contained dishes from 5 African countries
(Algeria, Cameroon, Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa) and we
recruited reviewers for each of these countries. We also constructed
a test suite of dishes from the US and recruited reviewers for this
region. Some reviewers had also submitted dish information in
the data collection phase. We had 52 community reviewers who
represented 6 different countries.

When exploring the use of Visual Question Answering (VQA) models
for uncovering potentially flattening and stereotypical outputs, we
use the template of questions and responses to probe the VQA models
detailed in Table F.8. The questions are also designed to understand
the composition of the image, and to identify specific customs around
the food, for example whether a drink or utensils are typically present
when the dish is served or eaten.

We present the following examples to demonstrate how the VQA
prompts were used with our generated images. We provide a rationale
for each question, highlighting its specific role in uncovering biases
and stereotypes present in food-related images. Some questions were

inspired by data points captured in our WWD dataset, while others
were informed by feedback from community reviewers. Notably,
these observations arose when we encountered instances where the
generated images are not of food; for example, of a human instead.

## G Further exploration of representational biases using weighted cosine similarity

## G.1 Formal definition of weighted cosine similarity

We measure the strength of association between a T2I image and a
descriptor by computing the weighted cosine similarity between
the image embedding and the descriptor textual embedding, in a similar manner to CLIPScore[31]. We use a CLIP [60] model to obtain
text embeddings for each descriptor prefixed with the prompt: “A
7
photo of {descriptor} food” and image embeddings for each
T2I dish image. We use clip-vit-base-patch32 as the CLIP model
to generate embeddings. To capture the direction of this association,
we assign a weight of +1 to positive descriptors (e.g. “delicious”)
and −1 to negative descriptors (e.g. “bland”) and multiply the cosine
similarity scores by these weights.8 The final score for each image is
calculated by averaging the weighted scores separately for positive
and negative descriptors, then finding the net difference between
these averages. This score is normalised to range between -1 and 1,
with scores closer to -1 indicating a stronger negative association and
scores closer to 1 indicating a stronger positive association. To analyse regional and model-specific trends, we disaggregate this metric
by averaging the generated image scores for each geographic region

## G.2 Descriptors used for the weighted cosine similarity experiments

We evaluate the association of generated images to a descriptor group
assessing dish image presentation. As explained in §3.2, we define a
list of keywords for the descriptor group through an iterative process,
starting with an initial seed of author-defined words that is refined
in consultation with community ambassadors. The presentation
descriptor focuses on the thematic and artistic visual characteristics
of the T2I images, such as whether they appear to depict *fine dining,*
*artisanal, or trendy* scenes. The complete list of keywords is shown
in Fig. G.15.

## G.3 Qualitative examples of the 10 images with the most positive food descriptor scores and the 10 images with the most negative food descriptor scores

We qualitatively review the “Top 10” T2I images with the highest
positive weighted cosine similarity scores (see Fig. G.16) and the
“Bottom 10” (see Fig. G.17) T2I images with the highest negative
weighted cosine similarity scores, both from DALL-E 2. Across both
lists, we observe that the weighted cosine similarity effectively captures differences in associations that are aligned with community
evaluations. T2I dish images with visually appealing backgrounds or
detailed food arrangements are assigned weighted cosine similarity
scores closer to +1 for the presentation descriptor group, indicating
a stronger association with positive food descriptors such as *fine-*
*dining*, *high-end*, and *fancy*. On the other hand, images with dark or
less visually appealing backgrounds receive lower weighted cosine
similarity scores for the food style descriptor, with values closer to

-1. These lower scores indicate a stronger association with negative food descriptors such as *cheap*, *weird*, and *greasy*, and correlate
strongly with community evaluations of the same images.

## H Large Language Model experiments

## H.1 Evaluating common knowledge understanding in LLMs

*Experiments.* Since our dataset contains key information about a
global set of dishes, as outlined in §2.2, this may be used to probe
LLMs to test their understanding of cuisines. We conducted experiments by querying OpenAI GPT 3.5 (knowledge cutoff September
2021), Turbo [55], Llama 3 (8B, knowledge cutoff March 2023), and
Llama 3 (70B, knowledge cutoff December 2023) [2] to predict the
following properties:

(i) Given a local dish name , predict the country of origin.

(ii) Given a local dish name and country , make a multiplechoice prediction of time of day eaten,

type of meal , and the utensils typically used.

(iii) Given a local dish name and country , predict a list of
ingredients for the dish.

*Evaluation.* Each of the LLMs is queried for each dish for tasks (i)-
(iii).9 The model predictions are first sanitised (e.g. in a Python-like
list format for ingredients) and then evaluated against the submitted
responses in the dataset. For instance, in (i), the column countries
in the WWD dataset contains a list of countries where this dish is
present. We check whether the country predicted by an LLM is
indeed contained in the list of countries from the dataset for each
of the 5 generations and for every dish. The accuracies for each
response category are computed separately for each continent. To
evaluate tasks (ii) and (iii), we chose the *Intersection over Union*
(IoU) metric, calculated as the ratio of the overlap between the list
predicted by an LLM and the submitted value to the volume of their
union. App. H.2 contains more details of the prompts used, as well

<sup>9</sup>5 seeds for GPT 3.5 and Llama 3 (8B). Llama 3 (70B) is on 1 seed, due to inference
time constraints.

Evaluation results of LLMs are presented in Table H.9. For all
the indicators and LLM models, there was a tendency for LLMs
to score lower for dishes from the African continent as compared
to dishes from other continents. For the utensils indicator, dishes
from Oceania also scored low. Due to the smaller sample size of
dishes from Oceania and South America, the results could be more
susceptible to noise, and therefore should be taken with a grain of
salt; however, the LLMs’ lower prediction scores for African dishes
is a clear demonstration of capability bias in the models. During
the evaluation process, we discovered that for certain dishes in the
WWD dataset, the LLMs suggest that the dishes are fictional or
made up. This was most prominent in dishes of African origin, but
was also observed in dishes from other continents, including North
America. This is problematic, since the dishes included in WWD
are real dishes input by community contributors and verified by
community reviewers. In App. H.3, we include an analysis of the
LLMs’ different failure modes.

## H.2 Prompts and sanitisation process

The following prompts were used to probe OpenAI GPT 3.5
Turbo [55], Llama 3 (8B), and Llama 3 (70B) [2] on their knowledge
of local dishes around the world.

Initial prompt: “Given an item of food called
local dish name , you are tasked with providing some answers about the common practices and common knowledge of this
dish.”

## Questions:

(2) Country: “Which country is local dish name from? Reply with just the country name.”

(1) Description: “What do you know about local dish name
from country ? Reply with a description of the dish.”

(3) Time of day: “What time of day is local dish name typically eaten in country ? Choose from the following: [‘breakfast’, ‘lunch’, ‘dinner’, ‘snack’, ‘anytime’, ‘other’] and return
as a python list of strings. You may choose multiple options.
Reply with just the list.”

(4) Type of meal: “What type of dish is local dish name
considered to be in country ? Choose from the following:
[‘Starter’, ‘Soup’, ‘Salad’, ‘Sauce’, ‘Side dish’, ‘Main dish - stand
alone (e.g. one pot meal)’, ‘Main dish - eaten with sides’, ‘Small
plate / bowl for sharing’, ‘Small plate / bowl served as a part of
a collection’, ‘Dessert’] and return as a python list of strings.
You may choose multiple options. Reply with just the list.”

(5) Utensils: “What type of utensils are used to eat local dish
name in country ? Choose from the following: [‘Knife’,

---

‘Fork’, ‘Spoon’, ‘Fingers’, ‘Right Hand’, ‘Left Hand’, ‘Chopsticks’, ‘Other food’, ‘Other’] and return as a python list of
strings. You may choose multiple options. Reply with just the
list.”

(6) Ingredients: “What are the ingredients for local dish
name from country ? List up to 10 most common ingredients. Reply only with a python list of ingredients, formatted
as [‘ingredient_1’, ‘ingredient_2’, ...].”

The time of day, type of meal, and utensils were designed as
multiple-choice questions with a fixed number of options. The LLMs’
answers were compared to the responses collected in the WWD
dataset, and the *Intersect over Union (IoU)* of the list of predictions
versus the list in the dataset was evaluated. Note that for the purpose
of computing the IoU, the options “other” and “other food” were
removed in the time of day and utensils analyses, since they can
introduce ambiguity in the analysis. In the analysis of utensils, the
“right hand” and “left hand” options were combined as “hand”. Keyword matching was used to compare the LLMs’ predictions against
the WWD data.

For the country name and ingredients, we needed to be more creative in the way we compared against the “ground truth” responses
in the WWD dataset, since the LLMs were tasked to predict these
as open-ended responses, rather than selecting the answers from
lists of options. Many countries or ingredients can have more than
one name or spelling, and a simple solution of keyword matching
is not sufficient to cover all possible variations. Therefore, we used
GPT 3.5 [11] as a string comparison tool to identify whether the two
strings are a match or not.

The following prompts are used to compare the two strings.

*Check if countries match:* “COUNTRY: llm_country \nCOUN-
TRIES: wwd_countries \nDoes the COUNTRY appear in COUN-
TRIES? Take into account that the same country may be referred to
in different variations. Answer with just True or False.”

*Intersect of ingredients:* “INGREDIENTS_A: llm_ingredients
\nINGREDIENTS_B: wwd_ingredients \nWhich ingredients appear in **BOTH** INGREDIENTS_A and INGREDIENTS_B? Take
into account that the same ingredient may be referred to in different
variations, and try to merge duplicates. Reply only with a python
list of ingredients, formatted as [’ingredient_1’, ’ingredient_2’, ...].”

*Union of ingredients:* “INGREDIENTS_A: llm_ingredients \n
INGREDIENTS_B: wwd_ingredients \nWhich ingredients appear
in **EITHER OR BOTH** INGREDIENTS_A and INGREDIENTS_B?
Take into account that the same ingredient may be referred to in
different variations, and try to merge duplicates. Reply only with a
python list of ingredients, formatted as [’ingredient_1’, ’ingredient_-
2’, ...].”

## H.3 Failures and problematic behaviour

Upon requesting that the LLMs generate a list of ingredients for
a given dish, there were some instances where the model refused
to produce a response in a format that we expected, i.e. a list. This
resulted in an exception when we tried to load and iterate through

the list as a Python object. Some of the issues were simple formatting errors (e.g. returning a bullet point instead of a Python list, or
forgetting to add quotation marks around each list item). For these
errors, we asked GPT 3.5 to reformat the responses in the correct
schema until the response could be loaded without any exceptions.

However, there are several non-trivial failure cases where the
responses could not be formatted into a list at all. Upon closer inspection of these failure cases, we discovered that these failures followed
a pattern and could be categorised into at least 4 different failure
modes, which we outline here with examples:

• “I apologize”: For both GPT 3.5 and Llama 3, the LLMs tend to
start with “I apologize” or “I’m sorry, but” when they cannot
directly respond to the user’s request. This in itself is not a
problematic failure mode.

Keywords: [“sorry”, “apologize”, “I’m afraid”, “unfortunately”]

Example sentence (GPT 3.5): “I apologize for any confusion, but as of now, there doesn’t seem to be any specific information available about a dish called ‘balugu’ from Uganda.
It’s possible that the dish is not a commonly recognized or
widely known dish in Ugandan cuisine. If you have any other
questions or need information on a different topic, feel free to
ask!”

• “Not known”: For some dishes, the models do not have
enough information about a dish to generate a response. Measuring the frequency of occurrence of this failure mode is
informative to understand the capability bias of the models.
While this failure mode is preferable over the model pretending to know about a dish and attempting to generate potentially false information, claiming that the dish is “not a known
dish” can be problematic, since it disregards and disrespects
the cultural value of said dish.

Keywords: [“not known”, “not a known”, “unknown”, “not
sure”, “no idea”, “no information”, “no data”, “I don’t know”, “I
don’t have”, “not widely known”, “not widely”, “n’t a known
dish”, “any known dish”, “any specific information”, “lesserknown”, “not well known”, “not well-known”]

Example sentence (GPT 3.5): “I’m sorry, but ‘khdawedj ala
darbouz’ is not a known dish in Algerian cuisine. It is possible that it may be a regional or local specialty, in which case
there may be limited information available about it. If you
have any other questions or if there is another dish you would
like to learn about, please feel free to ask.”

• “Not a real dish”: The most problematic failure mode of all is
when the model claims that the dish is made up or imaginary,
despite it actually being a real dish with a cultural association.
This was shockingly prominent as a failure mode, especially
for Llama 3 (70B) model, despite the results in Table H.9 indicating that Llama 3 (70B) has a better understanding of food
than Llama 3 (8B)—which may imply that the model is becoming overconfident in its judgments.

Keywords: [“not real”, “fictional”, “fictitious”, “imaginary”,
“not exist”, “don’t exist”, “not a real”, “made-up”, “made up
dish”]

Example sentence (Llama 3–8B): “I’m not familiar with
‘Aliwa tizalfawen’ from Algeria, as it seems to be a fictional
